config.heading: Facing these common organizational development challenges?
description: If any of these sound familiar, you are in good company. Most enterprises hit the same wall: a sound strategy that the organization itself is not built to deliver.

The plan is clear, but the organization around it is not aligned to it. Structure, culture, leadership and incentives were shaped for how the business used to run, so they quietly work against where it is going. Organizational development consulting is what realigns the whole system to the strategy, turning scattered fixes into lasting organizational effectiveness.

cards.title: Strategy that stalls in execution
cards.description: A clear plan on paper that the organization keeps failing to deliver in practice.

cards.title: Organizational culture that resists the strategy
cards.description: The way work really gets done pulls against where leadership is trying to take the business.

cards.title: Organizational structure that slows decisions
cards.description: Unclear roles and tangled reporting lines slow decisions and blur who owns what.

config.heading: The Edstellar organizational maturity model.
config.subheading: Five stages of organizational maturity. Edstellar moves your organization up the curve, level by level, until adapting to change becomes self-sustaining.

levels.title: Reactive
points: Change happens in reaction to crises
levels.description: The organization changes only when it has to. Restructures follow a crisis, culture is whatever it grew into, and structure is inherited from how the business used to run. Alignment to the strategy is accidental. The move to Repeatable begins the moment the operating model, roles and decision rights are defined on purpose.

levels.title: Repeatable
levels.description: Now there is order. Structure, processes and governance are clear and roles are defined. What is missing is direction, because the organization is built for stability rather than for the strategy, and it is slow to shift when priorities move. Reaching Realigned means designing structure, culture and leadership around what the strategy actually requires.

levels.title: Realigned
points: The org is built to execute
levels.description: The organization is built to execute. Structure follows strategy, leadership is set up to drive it, and the culture supports rather than resists it. The gap now is adaptability: the design is right for today, but the organization cannot yet sense and adjust as conditions change. Responsive is where measurement and feedback close that loop.

levels.title: Responsive
levels.description: Organizational health is managed with evidence. Culture, capability and readiness are measured, and the organization adjusts structure and leadership on data rather than opinion. The last step is as much cultural as structural, because the organization starts renewing itself every cycle without depending on outside help.

levels.title: Regenerative
points: The org renews itself each cycle
levels.description: The organization runs as an engine for its own change. It senses where it is drifting out of alignment, redesigns, embeds the change and reinvests, cycle after cycle. Alignment compounds, change lives in how the organization works rather than in a few leaders, and shows up as a genuine source of advantage.

config.expand_title: The model is a path, not a scorecard you fill in once. Each level is a genuine step change from the one before, so here is what each stage looks like and what it takes to reach the next.

business_meaning.title: What it means for the business.
business_meaning.text: The higher you climb, the more it shows where the business feels it: faster execution when strategy shifts, stronger internal mobility and succession, and change effort you can defend with evidence rather than activity. Near the top of the curve, the organization stops reading as a constraint on strategy and starts working as the thing that delivers it.

items.question: What does change management consulting include?
items.answer: This organizational change management engagement covers your change strategy and case for change, stakeholder and impact assessment, communication and engagement, training and enablement, resistance management, and the adoption metrics and reinforcement that make it stick, all aligned to the business goal.

items.question: How is change management different from project management?
items.answer: Project management delivers the solution on time and on budget. Change management handles the people side of change, making sure people actually adopt it, by managing the stakeholders, communication and reinforcement that turn a delivered project into new ways of working.

items.question: How long does a change management engagement take?
items.answer: It runs alongside the change it supports, from a few weeks for a focused rollout to several months for a large transformation, depending on scale and how many groups are affected.

items.question: Do you deliver the change, not just plan it?
items.answer: Yes. Communication, training and the reinforcement that embeds new ways of working are a core part of the engagement, so the change becomes how people actually work.

items.question: What do we get at the end?
items.answer: A change strategy, a stakeholder and impact map, a communication and engagement plan, an enablement plan and the adoption metrics you own and run.

items.question: What change management model or framework do you use?
items.answer: Every engagement runs on Edstellar's own 5A method. It is grounded in proven change models, Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze, Kotter's 8-step process and the ADKAR adoption model, synthesized into one practical approach so your change is handled systematically rather than by the textbook.
